It is an all-industry, all-size, all-cyber measure, not BEC-specific or mid-market-financial-services-specific. Preserve these limitations when using it as a BEC frequency bridge.

sources.title: MYOB mid-sized business cyber attack survey 2024
sources.usage_notes: Use as an Australian mid-sized business (20-500 FTE, revenue over AUD 5M) cyber-attack prevalence source. Survey by Dynata for MYOB, fieldwork 22 March - 15 April 2024, n=593. Reports 60% of mid-sized businesses and 81% of finance and insurance mid-sized businesses experienced a cyber attack. Commercial vendor survey (lower trust than official statistics), all-cyber not BEC-specific. Figure accessed via CFOtech reporting of the MYOB survey.

sources.title: Cybersecurity Insiders 2024 Insider Threat Report
sources.usage_notes: Use as an organization-level insider-attack prevalence source. Reports that 76% of organizations experienced insider attacks in 2024, up from 66% in 2019. Vendor-sponsored survey (lower trust than official statistics); "insider attacks" is broad and includes negligent and careless insiders, not only deliberate misuse. Preserve these limitations when using it as a frequency bridge.

sources.title: Gurucul 2026 Insider Risk Report
sources.usage_notes: Use as an organization-level insider-incident prevalence source. Survey of 725 IT and security professionals conducted in late 2025; reports that only 10% of organizations had zero insider incidents in the past 12 months (i.e. 90% experienced at least one), up from 83% (17% zero) in 2024. Vendor-sponsored survey (lower trust than official statistics); "insider incidents" is broad and includes negligent insiders, not only deliberate misuse. Preserve these limitations when using it as a stress bridge.

sources.title: BCI Supply Chain Resilience Report 2024
sources.usage_notes: Use as an organization-level supply-chain disruption prevalence source (~80% of organizations experienced a disruption in the past year; 43.6% cite third-party failure as the top cause). Broad supply-chain disruption (all causes), not third-party-only, and not sector- or size-specific. Preserve these limitations when using it as a third-party-outage frequency bridge.

sources.title: Interos Annual Global Supply Chain Report (Resilience 2022)
sources.usage_notes: Use as supply-chain disruption event-frequency context (organizations faced on average three major supply-chain events in the last 12 months, costing an average of USD 182M). Vendor survey; all-cause supply-chain events, not third-party-only. Supports a near-ceiling stress frequency via an interpretive multi-event conversion, not a directly reported prevalence.

sources.title: SPF Business Email Compromise scam interception case 2024
sources.usage_notes: Use as a documented Singapore BEC single-event loss. A Singapore-based investment banking firm initiated transfers of about USD 6.66M to a scammer on 19-20 September 2024; SPF and US authorities intercepted over USD 5M. One documented extreme case, not a loss distribution or a mid-market average; the gross transferred amount is modeled, gross of recovery.

sources.title: IBM Report: Canadians' Data Security Under Increased Threat, While Breach Costs Surge
sources.usage_notes: Primary IBM Canada newsroom release for the 2025 Cost of a Data Breach report. Provides the Canada national average breach cost (CA$6.98M in 2025, up from CA$6.32M in 2024) and a Canada financial-sector figure (CA$9.97M). The national average is all-sector and enterprise-weighted, so treat it as a Canada-specific likely-cost anchor with a mid-market applicability caveat, not a mid-market-specific loss table. It replaces the low-confidence ITPro secondary bridge for the Canada likely-impact anchor.

sources.title: Rapport IBM 2025 : coût d'une violation de données en France
sources.usage_notes: Primary IBM France newsroom release for the 2025 Cost of a Data Breach report. States the France national average breach cost (EUR 3.59M in 2025, down ~7% from 2024) and a France financial-services sector figure (EUR 4.65M), based on 34 French organizations breached between March 2024 and February 2025. The national average is all-sector and enterprise-weighted, so treat it as a France-specific likely-cost anchor with a mid-market applicability caveat, not a mid-market-specific loss table. It replaces the global IBM average bridge for the France likely-impact anchor. EUR values normalize to USD via the reviewed ECB EUR/USD assumption in calibrations/fx_rates.yaml.

intended_use: France data breach frequency by enterprise size class
sources.title: Eurostat ISOC_CISCE_IC - ICT security incidents by size class (France)
sources.usage_notes: Official EU statistics. Indicator E_SEC2ICNF is the percentage of enterprises that experienced an ICT security incident leading to disclosure of confidential data (any cause). France 2024 values by size: 10-49 = 1.98%, 50-249 = 3.83%, 250+ = 7.3%. CRITICAL CAVEAT: the survey population is "all activities except the financial sector" (nace_r2 = C10-S951_X_K), so this is a non-financial-sector proxy applied to a financial-services shard; financial services are typically more targeted, so it likely understates. It is also self-reported and narrower than "any cyberattack." Used for frequency min (small) and likely (medium); the JSON query returns the exact values in the gathered bytes.

intended_use: France data-theft consequence prevalence (stress frequency anchor)
sources.title: CESIN 11e Barometre annuel de la cybersecurite des entreprises (2025)
sources.usage_notes: CESIN 11th annual barometer, fielded by OpinionWay among ~397 French RSSI/CISO members (Nov-Dec 2025). Headline figures: 40% of surveyed firms suffered at least one significant cyberattack in 2025 (50% among large enterprises), and data theft was the leading technical consequence, cited by 52% of attacked firms. CAVEATS: the sample skews large (43% ETI, 40% large enterprises), it measures any significant cyberattack rather than data breach specifically, and the data-theft prevalence used as a stress anchor is derived (0.40 x 0.52 ~= 0.21). The CESIN primary is a PDF communique; the exact figures are byte-verifiable in named trade coverage (Le Monde Informatique, itforbusiness, Global Security Mag). Used only as an upper stress anchor for France frequency.max, never the central value.

intended_use: France economy-wide breach cost lower bound
sources.title: Asteres - Le cout des cyberattaques reussies en France (2022)
sources.usage_notes: Asteres economic study (for CRIP). Reports the average cost of a successful cyberattack in France at EUR 58,600 (direct cost EUR 25,600 excluding ransom), and estimates the 2022 total cost at EUR 2bn. Used only as a conservative France-specific impact.min floor. CAVEATS: it is an economy-wide average across all organization sizes and all cyberattack types (not data-breach-specific or financial-services-specific), and an average rather than a true minimum quantile. EUR normalizes to USD via the reviewed ECB EUR/USD assumption. Figure verified in the gathered PDF text.

intended_use: France data breach regulatory stress anchor
sources.title: GDPR Article 83(5) maximum administrative fine (via CNIL)
sources.usage_notes: CNIL statement of the GDPR Article 83(5) maximum administrative fine for the most serious breaches: EUR 20 million or 4% of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher (page states "20 millions" and "4 %"). For a mid-market firm the EUR 20M absolute cap is the binding ceiling, used as a France/EU regulatory impact.max stress anchor (mirrors the UK FCA-penalty and AU Privacy-Act-cap pattern). CAVEAT: a statutory maximum penalty cap, not a total event-loss estimate, expected loss, or claims severity. EUR normalizes to USD via the reviewed ECB EUR/USD assumption.

sources.title: SPF Annual Scam and Cybercrime Brief 2025
sources.usage_notes: Singapore's national police statistics for reported scams. Reports 377 business email compromise cases and SGD 35.3M lost in 2025, against 368 cases and SGD 88.5M in 2024. Use to derive a Singapore-specific average loss per reported BEC case, replacing US complaint data used as Singapore context. Reported cases only, so it is an incidence floor; covers all sectors, not financial services specifically; losses swung 60% year on year, so a single year is not a stable central estimate.
